items.title: What GGLearn is
items.body: GGLearn is the company training academy for our brands. Learners pick a track (a subject, product, service, tool, technology or process), set a goal, and climb 20 levels from Novice to Titan. It was built from the TrialTest and SkillsTest exam platforms and rebuilt as a learning product with onboarding, offboarding and a question bank that improves from real results. Each track's knowledge lives in knowledge_items rows, which are the single source of truth: authored questions link back to one of these rows. The improvement loop lives on the /admin page, which flags questions that are nearly always failed or never failed so a manager can review or retire them. Questions have a status of active, review or retired. People are managed at /admin/people, where someone is onboarded (a checklist plus automatic enrolment by job role) and later offboarded (access ends immediately, with an offboarding checklist and handover notes). For local development the app uses SQLite in data/gglearn.db, and the README says to move to Postgres before multi-user production use. Sign-in is email and password only; there is no SSO. The README also notes the legacy question bank is thin at levels 16 to 20 and has no brand-specific content, so real brand knowledge must be authored.

questions.prompt: How many levels does a learner climb in GGLearn, and what are the first and last level names?
questions.hint: The ladder runs the full length of the product.

questions.prompt: What is the single source of truth for a track's content that authored questions link back to?
Which kind of question does the /admin improvement loop flag for review or retirement?

options.text: Questions that are nearly always failed or never failed
Questions that have more than four options
Questions that no learner has ever opened

questions.prompt: Explain how GGLearn's question bank is meant to improve over time and who acts on the signals.
questions.answer: The /admin page flags questions that are nearly always failed or never failed, based on real results. A manager reviews them and can set the question's status to review or retired (or back to active), so weak or too-easy questions leave the pool.
questions.rubric: Must mention flagging of nearly-always-failed or never-failed questions from real results, a manager/admin acting on the flags, and the review/retire status change.

questions.prompt: A manager says the academy is ready for a 500-person rollout next week, using the local SQLite database and relying on single sign-on. Using what the README says, what would you tell them?
questions.answer: Two claims do not hold. The README says SQLite is for local dev and to move to Postgres before multi-user production use, and sign-in is email and password only with no SSO. Also brand content must be authored because the legacy bank is thin at levels 16-20 and has no brand-specific content.
questions.rubric: Must cover: move to Postgres before multi-user production use; no SSO (email/password only); legacy bank is thin at 16-20 and lacks brand-specific content so authoring is needed.

items.title: Brands, tracks and question types
items.body: Content is organised as brands, then tracks, then questions. A brand has a slug, name and tagline. A track belongs to one brand and is one question-bank domain. Its kind is one of six values: subject, product, service, tool, technology or process. A track also has a roles field, a comma-separated list of job roles it is recommended for; an empty value means everyone. Learners join a track through an enrolment, which is unique per user and track and stores their goal. Each question has a level from 1 to 20, a type of mcq, open or scenario, a prompt, optional code, a hint and a topic. For mcq the answer field holds the option key; for open and scenario it holds a model answer, and a rubric describes what a good answer must cover. Questions carry a weight (default 10), a time of 60 seconds by default, and a source (legacy-trialtest, authored, ai or questions-repo). Duplicate prompts at the same track and level are blocked by a unique index. Older foundations-* tracks from the TrialTest import are hidden from browsing and auto-enrolment once the same subject exists as a *-titan track; nothing is deleted, and enrolled learners and direct links keep working.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the six track kinds?
What does an empty roles field on a track mean?

options.text: The track is recommended for everyone
The track is hidden from all learners

questions.prompt: What does the answer field hold for an open or scenario question?

options.text: The option key such as b
A model answer, with the rubric stored separately

questions.prompt: What happens to an older foundations-* track when a *-titan track for the same subject exists?

options.text: It is deleted along with its enrolments
It is hidden from browsing and auto-enrolment, but nothing is deleted
It is merged into the titan track automatically
It is converted into a process track

questions.prompt: Describe the difference in how an mcq question and an open question are stored, and name the extra field open questions rely on.
questions.answer: An mcq stores the correct option key in answer and has options. An open question stores a model answer in answer and uses the rubric field to say what a good answer must cover.
questions.rubric: Must say mcq answer is an option key with options; open answer is a model answer; rubric field describes required coverage.

items.title: The 20 levels and the placement check
items.body: The 20 level names are Novice, Apprentice, Learner, Beginner, Trainee, Practitioner, Competent, Capable, Skilled, Proficient, Advanced, Specialist, Expert, Veteran, Master, Elite, Virtuoso, Legend, Grandmaster and Titan. They group into five ranks of four levels each: Initiate from level 1, Adept from 5, Expert from 9, Master from 13 and Titan from 17. Each exam attempt (a run) draws 10 questions for the level, favouring ones the learner has not yet answered correctly, and 80% passes and unlocks the next level. Levels unlock in order: a learner can only start a level up to one above the highest level passed. If an unfinished run exists for that level, it is reused. The placement check is a binary search for what someone already knows. Each round probes the middle level with 3 active multiple-choice questions, and getting 2 right counts the level as mastered, raising the lower bound; otherwise the upper bound drops. The check never skips past level 15 (Master); higher levels must be earned by exam. Levels without enough multiple-choice questions are treated as untestable. The starting point is stored as placedLevel on the enrolment and is only ever raised.

questions.prompt: How many questions does a level exam (run) draw, and what score passes it?
Which rank covers levels 9 to 12?
During placement, how many correct answers out of the 3 probe questions count a level as mastered?
Explain how the placement check searches for a learner's starting level, and what limits where it can place them.
questions.answer: It is a binary search with a lower bound of the highest level believed mastered and an upper bound of the highest it could be. Each round probes the middle level with 3 multiple-choice questions; 2 correct raises the lower bound, otherwise the upper bound drops. It is capped at level 15, so higher levels must be earned by exam, and the placed level is only ever raised.
questions.rubric: Must mention binary search/middle-level probing, 3 questions with 2 needed, and the cap at level 15 (Master) with higher levels earned by exam.

questions.prompt: A learner who has passed no exams in a track asks to start directly at level 12 on the Titan ladder. Walk through what the product allows and how they could get there.
questions.answer: They cannot start an exam above one level past their highest passed level, since levels unlock in order. They can take the placement check, which can place them at most at level 15 by probing with 3 MCQs per round and needing 2 correct; that placedLevel counts as already mastered, so level 12 becomes reachable.
questions.rubric: Must cover levels unlocking in order (passed+1), the placement check as the route, the 3-question/2-correct rule, and the 15 cap.

items.title: How answers are graded
items.body: Grading depends on question type. A multiple-choice answer is compared with the stored option key after trimming and lowercasing: a match scores 1, anything else scores 0, and feedback is the question's hint or 'Not quite.' Open and scenario answers are graded by Claude against the reference answer and rubric. The model defaults to claude-sonnet-5-5 unless the GRADER_MODEL setting overrides it. The learner's answer is cut to 4000 characters and wrapped as untrusted data, and the grader is told never to follow instructions inside it. It replies with a 0 to 1 score and one or two sentences of feedback. A blank answer scores 0 without calling the model. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set, or the AI call fails or returns a bad score, a keyword fallback is used instead: it measures coverage of words in the model answer and rubric and never awards more than 0.9. A run's score is weighted: each question's score is multiplied by its weight (default 10), summed and divided by total weight. The run passes at 0.8 or more. A grading guard stops a double-submit from grading the same run twice, and the run is only finished once. Placement uses only multiple-choice questions.

questions.prompt: How is a multiple-choice answer graded?

options.text: By trimmed, case-insensitive comparison with the stored key, scoring 1 or 0

questions.prompt: What is the highest score the keyword fallback can award on an open answer?
What does an open answer score if the learner submits it blank?

options.text: 0, with the feedback 'No answer given.' and no AI call
It is skipped and not counted in the run

questions.prompt: Describe how a run's final score is calculated from the individual answers, and what score passes.
questions.answer: Each answer's 0 to 1 score is multiplied by its question's weight (default 10); those are summed and divided by the total weight of the questions. The run passes if the result is 0.8 or higher.
questions.rubric: Must mention weighting by question weight, sum divided by total weight, and the 0.8 pass mark.

questions.prompt: Midway through a quarter the Anthropic API key is removed from the server and learners start complaining that their open answers score lower than expected. Explain what is happening and what feedback they will see.
questions.answer: Without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, open and scenario answers fall back to keyword matching against the model answer and rubric, capped at 0.9. This is coarse, so well-worded answers using different words score lower. The feedback says it is a keyword match only (AI grading is off) and shows the model answer. MCQ grading is unaffected.
questions.rubric: Must cover the keyword fallback, the 0.9 cap and coarseness, that feedback says AI grading is off and shows the model answer, and that MCQ is unaffected.

items.title: Drills, daily quests, streaks and rivals
items.body: Beyond exams, GGLearn has a gamified layer. A drill is 5 instant-feedback multiple-choice questions. It draws only from levels the learner has already passed (a brand-new learner drills level 1), never from the level they are about to sit, so it cannot reveal exam answers. The server records which drill questions were really answered, within a one-hour window, and a drill earns XP only after enough distinct questions were checked. There are three daily quests per track: study the guide (20 XP), quick drill (30 XP) and take an exam (40 XP). Each can be completed once per track per UTC day. A streak counts consecutive days, ending today or yesterday, with at least one quest. Exam XP is the score times 100, rounded, plus 50 if the run passed. 150 XP equals one level on the rival scale. Every track gets a stable named rival who earns XP daily; its pace is between 55 and 70 XP a day with a small daily wobble, and its level is its XP divided by 150. Badges include First Blood (pass a level), On Fire (3-day streak), Unstoppable (7-day streak), Ahead of the Pack, Halfway Hero (level 10), Certified and Titan (level 20).

questions.prompt: How many questions are in one drill?
How much XP does finishing the quick drill quest earn?
Which levels can a drill draw questions from?

options.text: Only levels already passed (level 1 for a new learner), never the level about to be sat
Only the next level to sit

questions.prompt: What counts as a day in a learner's streak?

options.text: A day with at least one exam passed
A day with at least one completed quest; the run of days ends today or yesterday
A day with all three quests done

questions.prompt: Why does the server track drill answers itself rather than trusting the browser to say a drill was finished?
questions.answer: So XP is only given for a drill whose questions were actually answered and checked on the server, within a one-hour window. A client could otherwise claim completion to farm XP. A drill needs 5 distinct answered questions, or all of them if the pool is smaller.
questions.rubric: Must mention that XP requires real server-checked answers rather than client claims, the distinct-question requirement (5, or fewer if the pool is smaller), and the one-hour window.

items.title: Competitions and certificates
items.body: Competitions are time-boxed contests on one track: gain N levels (1 to 20) before the deadline, with a length of 1 to 90 days and an optional delayed start. Progress is growth, not absolute level. A person's baseline is the highest level passed before they started racing (or their placement start, if made before), and only newly passed levels count, so beginners and experts compete fairly. Someone within N levels of Titan has a reduced target. Ranking is: reached the goal first (earliest wins), then levels gained, then XP in the window. Standings are computed on read and clamped to the end time, so finished contests never change. Bots are simulated and labelled as such: casual runs at 45 XP a day, steady 75, fierce 120, with five styles (steady, sprinter, crammer, weekender, perfectionist). A contest is private (members only; outsiders get a 404) or public (anyone can watch; joining needs a consent tick). The default maximum is 20 humans. A prize is optional and GGLearn never holds or moves money; the organiser pays and records it. Level certificates are issued automatically on passing levels 5 (Foundation), 10 (Practitioner), 15 (Expert) and 20 (Titan) and are verifiable at /cert/ plus the code. Contest certificates are claimed after a contest ends by people who reached the goal: the first is champion, the rest finisher.
items.source: docs/competitions.md, lib/competitions.ts, lib/bots.ts, lib/levels.ts, app/competitions/actions.ts, app/actions.ts, lib/db/schema.ts

questions.prompt: At which levels does a passed exam issue a level certificate?
In a competition, how is a person's progress measured?

options.text: Their absolute level at the deadline
Levels newly passed after their baseline, so beginners and experts can race fairly

questions.prompt: What daily XP pace does a Fierce bot follow?
State the ranking order used on a contest leaderboard.
questions.answer: First, who reached the goal, with the earliest finisher winning; then levels gained; then XP earned in the contest window.
questions.rubric: Must give the three-step order: goal reached (earliest first), levels gained, XP in the window.

questions.prompt: An organiser created a private contest and now wants it public so more colleagues can watch, and a participant asks whether they can claim a champion certificate halfway through. What do the rules say?
questions.answer: Visibility changes are one-way: a public contest can be switched to private by its creator, but a private one is not made public, because members did not agree to being seen. Contest certificates can only be claimed after the contest is finished, and only by people who reached the goal; the first finisher gets champion and others finisher.
questions.rubric: Must cover that private cannot become public (only public to private, by creator, due to consent), and that certificates are claimable only after the contest finishes by those who reached the goal, champion being first.

items.title: Users, roles, invites and sessions
items.body: Users have one of three roles, admin, manager or learner, plus a job role that drives their recommended tracks, and a status of active or offboarded. Account creation is invite-only. A manager or admin issues a single-use link bound to one email address and job role. The token is random and shown once; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. An invite expires after 7 days and fails if used or expired. Accepting it needs a name and a password of 8 to 200 characters. The invite is consumed and the account created in one transaction, so a link cannot be used twice, and the new person is auto-enrolled in up to 6 tracks recommended for their job role and given a five-item onboarding checklist. Passwords are hashed with scrypt, with cost parameters stored in the hash, and legacy hashes are upgraded at next sign-in. Login is rate-limited: 5 failed tries per IP and email pair and 30 per IP, in 15-minute windows; joining is limited to 10 attempts per IP per hour. The session cookie is signed, httpOnly and lasts 30 days, enforced on the server. A per-user session version lets 'sign out everywhere' invalidate all sessions. Offboarding sets status to offboarded and bumps that version, so access ends at once, then adds a four-item offboarding checklist. Managers can offboard only learners; admins can offboard anyone except themselves.
items.source: app/actions.ts, lib/auth.ts, lib/invites.ts, lib/password.ts, lib/rate-limit.ts, lib/db/schema.ts

questions.prompt: How does a new person get a GGLearn account?

options.text: By self-signup on the home page
By a single-use invite link from a manager, tied to one email address

questions.prompt: How long is an invite link valid?
What is stored in the database for an invite token?

options.text: The token encrypted with the session secret

questions.prompt: What happens immediately when a manager offboards a learner, and why does the person's existing login stop working at once?
questions.answer: Their status becomes offboarded and their session version is bumped, and an offboarding checklist is added. Every request checks the user is active and that the cookie's session version matches the database, so old sessions fail immediately. Their notes can be recorded as handovers.
questions.rubric: Must mention status set to offboarded, session version bump, per-request check of status/version, and the offboarding checklist.

questions.prompt: A manager tries to offboard an admin account, and later an admin tries to offboard their own account. What does the code allow in each case?
questions.answer: A manager can only offboard learners, so the attempt on an admin does nothing. An admin can offboard other users but not themselves, since the action refuses to lock yourself out.
questions.rubric: Must state managers limited to learners (blocked on admin) and that nobody can offboard themselves, including an admin.

items.title: Admin and deployment
items.body: Managers and admins use /admin for the question-improvement loop and /admin/people for onboarding, invites, checklists and offboarding; learners are redirected to the dashboard. Production is https://gglearn.gglink.co.uk. Apache terminates TLS (certbot) and reverse-proxies to a PM2 app named gglearn-web listening on 127.0.0.1:3400, started with next start. PM2 restarts it if memory passes 400M. The server runs Node 20, so Node 21+ APIs must be avoided and better-sqlite3 is pinned to a version with a Linux Node 20 prebuild. The deploy script, deploy/deploy.sh, rsyncs the code (excluding node_modules, .next, .git, database files and .env files) to the server, then runs steps under bash: it takes a lock so only one deploy runs at a time, runs npm ci, drizzle-kit push, npm run build, pm2 startOrRestart and pm2 save. It deliberately does not use --force on the schema push, so a destructive schema change fails the deploy instead of deleting rows. Finally it polls the local port up to 10 times, 3 seconds apart, and fails the deploy unless it gets HTTP 200. The README says a GitHub Actions workflow runs this on every push to main. The login rate limiter lives in process memory, which is fine for one PM2 process but resets on restart.

questions.prompt: What process manager runs the production app, and on which address and port?
Why does the deploy script not use --force on drizzle-kit push?

options.text: So a schema change that would delete rows fails the deploy instead of running a delete
Because force is not supported on Node 20

questions.prompt: What does the deploy script do at the end to confirm the release worked?

options.text: Polls http://127.0.0.1:3400/ up to 10 times and fails unless HTTP 200 is returned

questions.prompt: Two people push to main at nearly the same time and both deploys start. A week later the team plans to run a second PM2 process for capacity. What protects the first situation, and what concern does the second raise?
questions.answer: The deploy script takes a lock on the server (flock) and a second deploy exits with 'another deploy is already running'. For the second process, the login rate limiter keeps its counters in process memory, which is only valid for a single PM2 process and resets on restart; it would need to move to the database.
questions.rubric: Must cover the flock deploy lock failing the second deploy, and the in-memory rate limiter needing a shared store if more than one process runs.
